source: ACTMED authors (2025) Adaptive Clinical Test selection via Model-based Experimental Design
finding: Gap 1 partial. An LLM that picks tests itself (implicit selection) leans on globally popular tests. Code-side Bayesian selection picks tests per patient. It beat implicit selection, random selection and a fixed best subset on three tabular datasets, and even beat using all features on some sets.
numbers: 3 tests allowed. Datasets: hepatitis, diabetes, kidney. Models GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. 5 seeds. Implicit selection chose the global-best features almost exclusively, most on diabetes. Exact accuracy values sit in figures and were not read.
limits: Tabular risk prediction, not fault isolation. Outcome tables are LLM-simulated. Uniform test costs. Compares accuracy at a fixed 3 tests, not tests-to-solve, and not at equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Supports a code-side selector over free LLM choice. It is accuracy at a fixed budget, so gap 1 (tests needed at equal tokens) stays open.

source: ACTMED (2025) KL-based stopping and entropy versus KL selection
finding: Gap 2 and 7. A stop rule on expected belief change (stop when the next test is not expected to move the belief by a KL threshold) cut tests with equal or better accuracy than a fixed 3 tests. KL-based selection beat entropy-based selection.
numbers: At the conservative threshold the mean number of tests fell under two on all sets except hepatitis with GPT-4o; the paper says burden fell by nearly 50 percent. Table 3, GPT-4o-mini kidney: 1.60, 1.48, 1.28 tests at thresholds 0.3, 0.5, 0.7. GPT-4o kidney: 1.35, 1.09, 1.04. Table 6, GPT-4o-mini diabetes accuracy 0.593 (KL) vs 0.572 (entropy); kidney 0.992 vs 0.972.
limits: Baselines had no early stop, so the gain mixes the stop rule with selection. No ablation separates filter from scoring. Differences are small, 5 seeds.
agent_relevance: A cheap stop rule (expected belief shift below a threshold) can be tested on its own. Partly answers gap 7: stop on low expected change, not only on a singleton set.

source: Hartmann et al. (2026) Amortising Bayesian Experimental Design for Sequential Information Gathering in LLMs (ASIG)
finding: Gap 1 and 2 (token cost). Code-side BED (BED-LLM) is 25 to 36 times slower per episode than a plain LLM questioner. A fine-tuned policy rewarded with EIG matches plain runtime. On 14B models the gain over plain was only +4.2 and +1.8 points, and BED-LLM fell below the plain baseline on animals.
numbers: 20 Questions, 100 held-out entities per category (animals, plants), 5 episodes, 20-question budget. 7B: success more than doubled vs baseline. MediQ accuracy 14B: 54.1 to 54.2 percent; 7B baseline 46.7 vs ASIG 47.6 on one 7B row pair as printed (rows partly garbled).
limits: ICML workshop paper, non-archival. Needs fine tuning, which our no-training rule forbids. Simulated oracle LLM. Compute reported as wall clock, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Equal-token comparison matters: BED-style selectors cost an order of magnitude more inference. Our selector must be cheap (few candidates, one pass) or the token bill eats the gain.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) From Passive to Active Reasoning (AR-Bench), full text and appendix tables
finding: Gap 4. Where the answer space is large or open, planners that need a candidate list do not help. UoT was below zero-shot. Tree-of-thought and SFT were inconsistent. More rounds help early and then plateau.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy, detective cases / situation puzzles / guessing numbers: Llama-3.1-8B 31/43/0; 70B 40/54/8; 405B 43/55/12; GPT-4o-mini 62/41/6; GPT-4o 54/63/35; QwQ-32B 57/49/1. ToT on 8B: 45/53/2; on 70B: 40/52/14. SFT on guessing numbers: 0. Process score +7.7 percent in rounds 5-10, +2.5 percent in rounds 20-25.
quote: UoT relies on accurately defining the potential answer space and eliminating incorrect options.
limits: The paper explains UoT's failure by a large answer space (guessing numbers), an infinite one (situation puzzles) and hard option elimination (detective cases). That is the authors' account, not a tested cause. LLM-judged answers.
agent_relevance: Marks the edge of the closed-candidate assumption: the scaffold needs a candidate list that can be listed and tests that can eliminate members. For open faults it must first build and prune a list.

source: Besnard and Bastien-Toniazzo (1999) Expert error in trouble-shooting: an exploratory study in electronics (Int J Human-Computer Studies 50:391-405)
finding: Gap 6. A rare fault (short on condenser C7) looked like a common IC386 failure. Experts fixated on the IC. Novices tested more broadly and used fewer tests. Experts also ran chained tests on the same part instead of splitting.
numbers: 3 novices (2 years of technical school) vs 3 experts (19 to 20 years). Mean tests to cause: experts 39.33, novices 13. Tests of IC386: experts 18.66, novices 2. Share of tests on IC386: 47.45 vs 15.38 percent. Chained IC386 tests 5.36 vs 0. First IC test at 3.03 vs 23.07 percent of the diagnosis. One novice never found the fault. No statistics run.
limits: N=6, one circuit, one fault built to trap symptom matching. Authors call it exploratory and ran no ANOVA.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence that symptom matching fails on a look-alike rare fault. It suggests a switch trigger: a symptom-matched hypothesis that survives N tests without confirmation forces a normal-reference or split test. Not a measured threshold.

source: Besnard and Bastien-Toniazzo (1999) account of expert failure
finding: The authors explain the pattern as schema perseverance: symptoms launch a stored symptom-to-fault rule and revising it is slow. Both groups used surface cues. Novices used them to infer, experts to trigger an automated rule.
numbers: Same N=6 study. Paper cites Lesgold et al. 1988: expert radiologists were sometimes less accurate than residents.
limits: Mechanism is argued, not tested. Predictions were about direction only.
agent_relevance: Supports a fixation guard: count repeated tests on one component and force a different test type after a set number.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) FaulT-Bench, results text
finding: Gap 7. No agent has a criterion for concluding that no fault exists. They keep probing until a benign condition can be named as the root cause. The agent with the richest skills layer gave the most false faults.
numbers: 72 healthy-network tickets, 3 passes. False-fault rate: SADE 24 percent (51/210), ReAct 16 percent (33/209), Claude Code baseline 11 percent (21/198). Grounded-reasoning score on these: SADE 0.933, Claude Code 0.892, ReAct 0.845. 200 scenarios in total.
quote: What the agents lack is a criterion for concluding, with evidence, that no fault exists.
limits: Emulated networks, LLM-judge scoring, three agents. No stop-rule fix was tried; the paper only diagnoses.
agent_relevance: A stop rule needs an explicit no-fault exit: if every probed check matches the normal reference, answer no fault. Write the healthy-system readings before probing.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) FaulT-Bench, personas and cost
finding: Gap 7 and 8. Vague tickets raise false faults and cost. Agents spend most when the ticket is vague. Timeouts are costly. Real-fault runs are cheapest because the agent finds the fault, reports it and stops.
numbers: Pooled false-fault rate by ticket form: standard 17, naive 16, novice 31, naive-unsure 35, no-detail 47 percent; pooled outcome 0.820 down to 0.497. Claude Code no-detail: 30 tool calls vs 13 on correct-fault, 549k vs 136k tokens per answered run. 366 timeouts are 9 percent of 3,960 runs but 23 percent of US$1,525 spend; 36 percent of the Claude Code baseline budget went to runs with no diagnosis.
limits: Confounded with agent design. Costs are in dollars and tokens for whole runs, not per test.
agent_relevance: A turn cap with no stop rule wastes budget. A sufficiency stop plus a no-fault exit saves tokens, and a symptom-structuring intake step before the first test matters.

source: Wang and Hong (2025) Time Travel: LLM-assisted semantic behavior localization with git bisect, full text
finding: Gap 9. The paper scores bisect all-or-nothing, because one wrong verdict at any step invalidates the session. The base LLM judge reached 74.2 percent end to end, the fine-tuned one 80.6 percent.
numbers: 32 curated questions over three open-source repositories. All-or-nothing success 74.2 base, 80.6 fine-tuned (+6.4 points). Error-handling and safeguard changes were weakest. Developer study: 7 developers, 45.6 percent self-reported time saved.
limits: Single paper, small question set, self-reported time saving, fine-tuning used. It does not test verifying each split.
agent_relevance: Confirms the fragility but gives no result on a cheap check. Our check design must be tested; see d10.

source: Own calculation from Time Travel all-or-nothing figures (not a source)
finding: Gap 9, arithmetic only. If all-or-nothing success is the product of per-step verdict accuracies, a 5-step bisect at 74.2 percent implies about 94.3 percent per step. At 94.3 percent per step a 10-step bisect succeeds about 55 percent.
numbers: 0.742^(1/5)=0.943; 0.943^10=0.55. Assumes 5 steps and independent errors; neither is stated in the paper.
limits: Own derivation. Step count and independence are assumptions. Treat as a design hint.
agent_relevance: Candidate checks to test: vote of 3 verdicts only on surprising splits, or re-test both neighbours of the final boundary (2 extra checks).

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (SDBench), re-opened full text
finding: Gap 8 re-verified. Numbers in c20 and c21 hold. Test costs are US dollars; model inference is negligible ($0.15 per case). The saving came from questioning cheaply before ordering tests, not from refusing costly tests.
numbers: 304 NEJM cases (56 test set). Off-the-shelf o3 78.6 percent at $7,850. MAI-DxO with o3 81.9 percent at $4,735; 79.9 percent at $2,396; 85.5 percent at $7,184 with ensembling. 21 physicians, 764 diagnoses: 19.9 percent accuracy, 6.6 questions, 7.2 tests, $2,963, 11.8 minutes. Single vs batched mode both 83.9 percent on the test set.
quote: Dr. Stewardship did not reject expensive tests outright, but forced the panel to ask whether the same information could be acquired at lower cost.
limits: The gatekeeper is an LLM that may invent findings for tests not in the case. Physicians were barred from references, so 19.9 percent understates practice. Cases selected for difficulty.
agent_relevance: Cheap-first pays when test price dwarfs inference price. For our agent a test costs tokens and time, so that relation is reversed. Transfer is unproven.

source: Nori et al. (2025) SDBench worked example of a question replacing tests
finding: Gap 8. One case: baseline o3 anchored, ordered MRI and EEG, and was wrong at $3,431. The panel first asked about in-hospital toxin exposure, the patient confessed to hand sanitizer, and a targeted test gave the right answer at $795.
numbers: One worked case. Panel roles: Hypothesis, Test-Chooser, Challenger, Stewardship.
limits: Anecdote chosen by the authors. No ablation of which role gave the saving.
agent_relevance: Suggests an intake rule: ask observation and history questions before instrument tests, and name a disconfirming test. Not measured as a rule.

source: Grand et al. (2025, ICLR 2026) Shoot First, Ask Questions Later, full text re-opened
finding: Gap 2 and 1. Choosing questions by EIG alone gave tiny game gains. Choosing moves by Bayesian marginalisation over the answers gave the big gain. The lift came from the code that used the answers.
numbers: Targeting F1: Llama-4-Scout 0.367 (LM only) to 0.764 with full Bayes (question, move, decision); GPT-4o 0.450 to 0.782. Question rule alone: only +0.021 to +0.026 F1. GPT-5 LM-only 0.716 and it gained little. Full-Bayes small models won 0.82 to 0.83 vs humans; cost 1 percent of GPT-5 (Scout) and 35 percent (GPT-4o).
limits: Simulated spotter with fixed noise 0.1, closed board space. Reasoning-heavy models need no scaffold.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 2: most gain is from using answers correctly (update, eliminate, then act), not the question scoring rule. Invest first in belief-update code.

source: Grand et al. (2025) Battleship: redundant questions and budget use
finding: Gap 2. A filter for zero-gain questions works: zero-EIG (redundant) questions fell sharply when code scored the candidates. Strong players ask fewer questions.
numbers: Redundant questions (EIG=0): Llama-4-Scout 18.5 to 0.2 percent; GPT-4o 14.6 to 1.2 percent. Humans and GPT-5 ask 8.0 to 8.2 questions vs 14.1 to 14.9 for weak models. Weak models front-load all 15 questions; one-step lookahead evens this out.
limits: Filter effect is not separated from scoring: both sit in the same selection step.
agent_relevance: A zero-gain filter removes about one wasted test in six or seven for weak models; strong models need it less.

source: Schaafstal, Schraagen and van Berlo (2000) Cognitive task analysis and innovation of training: the case of structured troubleshooting (Human Factors 42:75-86), abstract page only
finding: Gap 5 partial. Technicians trained in structured troubleshooting (a general strategy plus a multi-level functional breakdown) solved about twice as many malfunctions, in less time, with less training time.
numbers: Ratio only: twice as many. Sample size and percentages are not on the page and were not read.
limits: ABSTRACT ONLY. The bundle mixes strategy and functional decomposition, so the effect cannot be credited to half-split. Full text not obtained.
agent_relevance: The trained method was functional decomposition plus a general cycle, not pure half-split. Supports giving the agent a functional breakdown of the system.

source: Search attempt log: Gugerty 2007 and Goldbeck et al. 1957
finding: Gap 5 stays open. The Gugerty (2007) record was blocked by Cloudflare, and the Goldbeck (1957) study was not reachable. The WebSearch budget ran out, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors, and arXiv search returned HTTP 429.
limits: Missing access, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Open: obtain the PDFs by hand or retry after rate limits reset.

finding: All reading used text from pdftotext. The shared drive filled to 0 bytes free during the run, so extracted text files were deleted after reading. Numbers above were copied while the text was open.
limits: Re-open sources to re-check any figure.
